question: What drew you to music technology specifically, rather than a pure performance or composition degree?
lookingFor: A genuine, specific motivation that shows the applicant understands music technology sits between music and engineering, not just 'I like music and computers'.

bullets: Point to a concrete moment or project that revealed the technical side of music to them
Distinguish the pull of music technology from pure performance or composition
Show they understand the discipline blends creative and technical skill
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've played guitar for years, but what really hooked me was recording my school band in a spare room and realising how much the mix changed how a song actually felt. I started messing with EQ and compression on cheap software and got obsessed with why a small tweak could make a flat recording suddenly sound alive. Pure performance never gave me that same buzz because I wanted to understand the machinery behind the sound, not just play it, and that's why music technology fits me better than a composition or performance route.

commonMistakes: Saying 'I love music and I'm good with computers' with no specific story
Describing pure performance ambitions with no technical angle
Not distinguishing music technology from adjacent degrees
followUps: What was the first piece of software or gear that made you want to go deeper into this?

question: Why did you choose our music technology course over other programs you could have applied to?
lookingFor: Specific, researched reasons tied to this course's studios, staff, or curriculum rather than generic praise.

bullets: Name a specific studio, module, piece of equipment, or staff research that matters to them
Connect that feature to something concrete they've already done or want to do
Show they compared this course against alternatives and made a real choice
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I looked at three courses, and yours was the only one with a dedicated module on live sound and immersive audio alongside the studio production side, which matters to me because I want to work across both recorded and live contexts. I also read about the surround sound suite you built two years ago, and I want to get hands-on with multichannel mixing, which I've only done in stereo so far on my own tracks. The other courses I looked at were much more composition-heavy, and I wanted somewhere that treats the engineering side as seriously as the creative side.

commonMistakes: Generic praise that could apply to any music tech course
Citing rankings or reputation with no specific detail
Confusing this course with a music production or sound engineering diploma elsewhere
followUps: What would you want to get out of that studio access in your first year?

question: Tell us about a track or project you've produced or recorded. Walk us through your process.
lookingFor: Concrete, hands-on experience with real technical decisions, not just a vague description of 'making music'.

bullets: Describe the actual workflow: recording, editing, mixing, or programming steps taken
Mention specific tools, plugins, or techniques used and why
Reflect honestly on what worked and what they'd change
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I produced a four-track EP with a friend who sings, recorded mostly on a single condenser mic into Reaper because that's what I could afford. The hardest part was the vocal takes, comping the best phrases together and then using a de-esser because she has quite sharp sibilance. For the mix I leaned on subtractive EQ before I ever reached for compression, which someone online recommended and which genuinely changed how clean my mixes sounded. If I did it again I'd treat the room better before recording, because I spent hours afterward trying to fix reflections I should have prevented.

commonMistakes: Vague claims of 'producing music' with no technical specifics
Listing software names with no explanation of what was actually done
No honest reflection on limitations or mistakes
followUps: What would you do differently if you recorded that same session again?

question: Which producer or audio engineer's work do you admire, and what specifically have you learned from studying it?
lookingFor: Evidence of active, critical listening beyond fandom, with specific technical observations.

bullets: Name a specific producer or engineer, not just an artist or band
Identify a specific technique or sonic signature they've noticed and can describe
Show they've tried to apply or test that observation in their own work
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I've spent a lot of time listening to how Jack Antonoff builds vocal spaces, particularly how dry and close the lead vocal sits against really lush, reverb-heavy backing layers. I read a few interviews where he talks about tracking vocals almost too close to the mic to get that intimacy, then contrasting it with big ambient pads. I tried imitating that on one of my own tracks by automating a tight, minimal-reverb lead against a wash of delayed guitar, and it taught me how much contrast, not just individual sounds, creates the feeling of depth in a mix.

commonMistakes: Naming a favourite artist rather than a producer or engineer
Describing admiration with no specific technical detail
No evidence of trying to apply the observation themselves
followUps: Have you tried recreating any technique of theirs yourself? How did it go?

subtopic: Music technology vs production vs composition
question: How would you describe the difference between music technology, music production, and sound engineering?
lookingFor: A clear, accurate sense of how these overlapping fields differ, showing the applicant understands what they're actually applying for.

bullets: Give a reasonable working distinction between the three, acknowledging overlap
Show music technology includes the underlying science and systems, not just the craft
Avoid treating the terms as fully interchangeable
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think of sound engineering as mostly the craft of capturing and shaping sound well, mic placement, gain staging, mixing decisions. Music production overlaps with that but also includes the creative and arrangement choices, deciding what the song needs. Music technology is broader again, it includes both of those but also the underlying systems, how digital audio actually works, building tools or instruments, coding for sound, which is why I'm drawn to it rather than a straight production diploma, I want the theory behind the craft as well as the craft itself.

commonMistakes: Treating the three terms as identical
Describing music technology purely as 'using software'
Giving no sense of where the fields actually overlap
followUps: Which of those three areas do you feel weakest in right now?

question: Can you explain what sample rate and bit depth actually mean, in your own words?
lookingFor: A correct, plain-language grasp of the two most basic digital audio concepts, showing genuine subject preparation.

bullets: Explain sample rate as how often the waveform is measured per second
Explain bit depth as how precisely each sample's amplitude is recorded
Give a real-world consequence of each, such as frequency range or noise floor
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Sample rate is how many times per second the analog sound wave gets measured and turned into a number, so 44.1kHz means it's sampled 44,100 times a second, and that rate determines the highest frequency you can actually capture accurately. Bit depth is about how much detail each of those measurements has, so a higher bit depth like 24-bit gives you a much wider range between the quietest and loudest sound you can represent without distortion or noise. I think of sample rate as the horizontal resolution of the waveform and bit depth as the vertical resolution.

commonMistakes: Confusing sample rate with bit depth or using the terms interchangeably
Giving only a definition with no practical consequence
Memorising a number like 44.1kHz with no understanding of why it matters
followUps: Why do you think 44.1kHz became the standard for CD audio?

question: What is the Nyquist theorem, and what happens if you try to record a frequency above the Nyquist limit?
lookingFor: An understanding of a genuinely technical concept beyond surface-level DAW use, showing readiness for the theoretical side of the course.

bullets: State that the sample rate must be at least twice the highest frequency you want to capture
Explain that going above that limit causes aliasing, where the frequency folds back and appears as a false lower frequency
Connect this to why anti-aliasing filters exist before analog-to-digital conversion
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: The Nyquist theorem says you need to sample at least twice as fast as the highest frequency you want to accurately represent, so at 44.1kHz you can capture up to around 22kHz cleanly. If a frequency above that limit sneaks in, it doesn't just get lost, it folds back down and shows up as a completely different, false frequency in the audible range, which is called aliasing and sounds like harsh, inharmonic noise. That's why audio interfaces have anti-aliasing filters before the analog-to-digital converter, to cut anything above the Nyquist frequency before it can cause that artifact.

commonMistakes: Not knowing the term aliasing or what it sounds like
Stating the theorem with no explanation of the consequence of violating it
Confusing aliasing with clipping or normal digital noise
followUps: Why might a studio choose to record at 96kHz instead of 44.1kHz if human hearing tops out around 20kHz?

question: What's the fundamental difference between an analog and a digital audio signal?
lookingFor: A clear grasp of continuous versus discrete representation and why conversion between them matters practically.

bullets: Describe analog as a continuous, unbroken representation of the sound wave
Describe digital as a series of discrete numerical samples approximating that wave
Give a practical example of where the conversion happens, such as an audio interface
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: An analog signal is a continuous electrical voltage that changes smoothly in exactly the same shape as the sound wave itself, like the groove on a vinyl record. A digital signal instead takes snapshots of that wave at regular intervals and stores each one as a number, so it's really an approximation rather than a perfect continuous copy. That conversion happens in the analog-to-digital converter inside an audio interface when you record a microphone, and it happens again in reverse, digital-to-analog, when you play audio back through speakers or headphones.

commonMistakes: Saying digital is 'more accurate' with no explanation of why
Not mentioning where or how the conversion physically happens
Confusing analog warmth claims with an actual technical explanation
followUps: Do you think analog gear still has a place in a mostly digital workflow, and why?

question: Can you explain how subtractive synthesis works?
lookingFor: A basic but accurate understanding of the oscillator, filter, and envelope signal chain that underpins most synthesizers.

bullets: Describe starting with a harmonically rich waveform from an oscillator
Explain that a filter removes or shapes frequencies to carve out the tone
Mention envelopes or LFOs shaping the sound over time
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Subtractive synthesis starts with an oscillator generating a waveform that's already rich in harmonics, like a sawtooth, and then you subtract from it using a filter, usually a low-pass filter that removes the higher frequencies to shape the tone. On top of that you've got an envelope, usually ADSR, controlling how the volume or filter cutoff changes over time, so a plucky sound has a fast attack and quick decay while a pad has a slow attack. I got into this by messing with a free synth plugin and just turning knobs until I understood what each stage was actually doing to the sound.

commonMistakes: Confusing subtractive synthesis with additive or FM synthesis
Naming the ADSR acronym with no explanation of what it does
Describing filters with no mention of what they actually remove
followUps: What's the difference between a low-pass and a high-pass filter, in terms of what you'd use each for?

question: How does FM synthesis differ from subtractive synthesis, and what kind of sounds is it good at making?
lookingFor: Understanding that FM synthesis generates complex timbres by modulation rather than filtering, plus practical awareness of its sonic character.

bullets: Explain that FM synthesis uses one oscillator to modulate the frequency of another, generating new harmonics
Contrast this with subtractive synthesis, which removes harmonics rather than generates them
Give an example of a sound or genre FM is known for
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Where subtractive synthesis starts rich and cuts frequencies away with a filter, FM synthesis builds complexity the opposite way, one oscillator, the modulator, rapidly changes the frequency of another, the carrier, and that interaction creates entirely new harmonics rather than just shaping existing ones. It's known for really bright, metallic, or bell-like tones, and for the classic digital electric piano sounds from the eighties, like on a DX7. I find it much harder to predict than subtractive synthesis because small changes in the modulation ratio can completely transform the timbre, which makes it fun but also a bit of a rabbit hole.

commonMistakes: Describing FM synthesis as just another type of filter shaping
No mention of the carrier and modulator relationship
Giving no example of what FM synthesis actually sounds like or is used for
followUps: Why do you think FM synthesis was harder for musicians to program than subtractive synths historically?

question: What's the difference between a MIDI file and an audio file?
lookingFor: A clear understanding that MIDI is performance instruction data, not sound, versus audio being an actual recorded waveform.

bullets: Explain MIDI as data describing notes, velocity, and timing, not actual sound
Explain audio as a recorded representation of an actual sound wave
Note that MIDI needs a sound source, like a synth or sample library, to actually make noise
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: An audio file is an actual recording, it's the sound wave itself captured as data, so a vocal take or a guitar recording is audio. A MIDI file isn't sound at all, it's instructions, like which note was played, how hard, and for how long, similar to sheet music in digital form. That's why the same MIDI file can sound completely different depending on what instrument or virtual synth you point it at, whereas an audio file always sounds like whatever was originally recorded.

commonMistakes: Saying MIDI files 'contain sound'
Not explaining that MIDI needs a sound source to be audible
Confusing MIDI with a specific type of instrument rather than a data protocol
followUps: Why is MIDI still useful in a modern production even though sample libraries can sound so realistic?

question: Explain what a compressor does and why an engineer might use one.
lookingFor: Practical understanding of gain reduction, threshold, ratio, and the creative or corrective reasons to compress a signal.

bullets: Explain that a compressor reduces the volume of a signal once it crosses a set threshold
Mention key parameters like ratio, attack, and release shaping how it responds
Give a real reason to use one, either evening out dynamics or adding character
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A compressor automatically turns down the level of a signal once it goes above a threshold you set, and the ratio controls how much it's turned down, so a 4 to 1 ratio means for every 4dB over the threshold, only 1dB actually gets through. Attack and release control how fast it clamps down and lets go, which changes the character a lot, a fast attack can tame transients while a slower one lets the initial punch through. I use compression mostly to even out a vocal that's naturally inconsistent in level, so quiet phrases sit closer to loud ones without me manually riding the fader the whole song.

commonMistakes: Describing a compressor as just 'making things louder'
No mention of threshold, ratio, attack, or release
Confusing compression with limiting with no distinction
followUps: What's the difference between a compressor and a limiter?

question: How would you approach EQing two instruments that are clashing in the same frequency range?
lookingFor: Practical mixing sense, showing they understand frequency masking and can describe a sensible corrective process, not just terminology.

bullets: Identify that the clash is likely a masking problem where both instruments fight for the same frequency band
Describe carving space by cutting one instrument where the other needs to sit, rather than boosting both
Mention using their ears and reference tracks, not just visual meters
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: If two instruments are clashing, say a bass guitar and a kick drum both fighting around 80 to 100Hz, my instinct is to decide which one needs to own that space and gently cut the other there rather than boosting either, because boosting both just makes the problem louder. I'd solo them together, not just individually, since the clash only shows up when they're playing at the same time. I try to use my ears first and treat the frequency analyser as a sanity check rather than the main tool, because two mixes can measure similarly and sound completely different.

commonMistakes: Suggesting boosting both instruments to make them 'stand out'
Relying entirely on a visual spectrum analyser with no mention of listening
Not recognising the clash as a masking problem
followUps: What other instrument pairs commonly clash in the frequency spectrum?

question: What's the difference between a condenser and a dynamic microphone, and when would you choose one over the other?
lookingFor: Practical recording knowledge about microphone types and appropriate use cases, not just naming the categories.

bullets: Explain the basic mechanical difference, such as condenser needing power and being more sensitive
Describe dynamic mics as more rugged and better suited to loud sources
Give a real recording scenario for each choice
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: A condenser microphone uses a charged capacitor plate that's very sensitive to small changes in air pressure, which makes it great at capturing detail and high frequencies, but it needs phantom power and can be easily overloaded by very loud sources. A dynamic mic uses a moving coil and magnet, it's less sensitive and captures less detail, but it can handle much higher sound pressure levels without distorting and it's more durable. I'd use a condenser on an acoustic guitar or a quiet vocal where I want detail and air, and a dynamic mic on a guitar amp or a snare drum where the sound is loud and I want something that can take a beating.

commonMistakes: Naming the two types with no explanation of the mechanical difference
Giving no practical example of when to use each
Confusing polar pattern with microphone type
followUps: What's a cardioid polar pattern, and why might you choose it for a vocal recording?

question: What causes latency in a digital recording setup, and how would you reduce it while tracking?
lookingFor: Understanding of buffer size trade-offs and practical fixes, showing real hands-on experience with recording software.

bullets: Explain that latency comes from the time it takes audio to travel through the interface's buffer for processing
Mention the trade-off between low latency and CPU strain, controlled by buffer size
Give a real fix, such as lowering buffer size while tracking or using direct monitoring
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Latency happens because the audio interface has to convert your signal to digital, send it through the buffer to the software, and back out again, and every step takes a small amount of time. The buffer size setting controls that delay directly, a smaller buffer means lower latency but asks more of your computer's processor, so it can cause crackling if you're running a lot of plugins. When I'm actually recording a performance I lower the buffer size as far as it'll go without glitching, and if that's still noticeable I use direct monitoring on the interface so I'm hearing the input signal itself rather than the round trip through the software.

commonMistakes: Not knowing what buffer size is or how it relates to latency
Suggesting there's no trade-off to lowering latency
Confusing latency with lag in an unrelated sense, like internet lag
followUps: Why might latency matter less when mixing than it does when tracking a live performance?

question: What is auditory masking, and why is it relevant to both mixing and audio compression formats like MP3?
lookingFor: Awareness that human hearing is not a neutral measuring instrument, and how that perceptual fact is exploited both creatively and technically.

bullets: Explain masking as one sound making another harder or impossible to perceive, usually when close in frequency or time
Connect it to practical mixing decisions, like why instruments fight for space
Connect it to lossy compression formats discarding masked frequencies to save data
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Auditory masking is when one sound makes another sound harder or impossible for us to actually hear, usually because they're close together in frequency or happening at almost the same moment, our hearing just can't resolve both clearly. In mixing that's exactly why two instruments in the same frequency range can clash, one effectively masks the other even if both are technically present in the recording. It's also the whole basis of formats like MP3, because the codec models what a human ear would mask anyway and just discards that data, which is how it shrinks file size without most listeners noticing much difference.

commonMistakes: Defining masking with no connection to a practical mixing or format example
Confusing masking with simple frequency clashing with no perceptual explanation
Not knowing that lossy compression formats rely on psychoacoustic modelling
followUps: Can you think of an example of masking happening in time rather than frequency?

question: Have you had any experience with programming environments for sound, like Max/MSP, SuperCollider, or Python, and what interests you about that side of the field?
lookingFor: Genuine curiosity about the computational side of music technology, honest about experience level rather than exaggerating it.

bullets: Give an honest account of actual experience, even if limited, rather than overstating it
Explain what specifically appeals about building tools or generative systems for sound
Show awareness that this is a distinct skill from using a DAW
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'm honestly still a beginner, I followed a few online tutorials in Pure Data building a simple granular synthesis patch, and it completely changed how I think about sound, because instead of using someone else's plugin I was deciding exactly how the grains were being sliced and reassembled. What appeals to me is that a DAW gives you a fixed set of tools, but writing code for sound means you can build an instrument or effect that doesn't exist yet if you can imagine it. I know that's a very different skill from mixing and I want to build it properly during the course rather than pretend I'm further along than I am.

commonMistakes: Claiming advanced coding skills with no ability to back it up under follow-up questions
Dismissing the coding side as irrelevant to 'real' music production
Vague enthusiasm with no specific example of what was tried
followUps: What's one thing you'd want to build if you had strong coding skills for sound?

question: AI tools can now generate full backing tracks or even vocals. How do you think this changes the role of a music technologist, and how do you feel about it?
lookingFor: Balanced, thoughtful reasoning about opportunity and risk rather than either uncritical excitement or blanket dismissal.

bullets: Acknowledge genuine opportunities AI creates, such as new sound design tools or faster workflows
Acknowledge genuine concerns, such as originality, consent, or job displacement
Land on a personal, reasoned position rather than a fence-sitting non-answer
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I think AI tools are genuinely useful as another instrument in the toolbox, I've used an AI stem separation tool to pull vocals out of an old reference track for sampling, and that would have been nearly impossible a few years ago. At the same time I'm uneasy about tools trained on artists' voices or styles without consent, because that feels like a real ethical line rather than just disruption. My honest position is that the technical craft of engineering, knowing why something sounds good and fixing it when it doesn't, becomes more valuable, not less, because taste and judgement are exactly what generic AI output still lacks.

commonMistakes: Either dismissing AI entirely or treating it uncritically as pure progress
Giving a vague non-answer with no personal position
Not mentioning any ethical dimension, such as consent or originality
followUps: Would you personally use an AI-generated vocal or instrumental in a project of your own? Why or why not?

question: If you wanted to sample a piece of another artist's recording in a track of your own, what would you actually need to consider?
lookingFor: Basic awareness of copyright and clearance issues around sampling, showing professional and ethical maturity, not just technical know-how.

bullets: Recognise that both the recording and the underlying composition may need separate clearance
Mention that uncleared sampling can have real legal and financial consequences
Show awareness of alternatives, like royalty-free sources or getting explicit permission
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd need to think about the fact that a sample usually involves two separate copyrights, the actual sound recording and the underlying song itself, so I might need permission from both the label and the publisher or songwriter. I learned this the hard way when I put a sampled loop in a track I uploaded and it got flagged and muted automatically online, which made me realise how seriously this is enforced even for small creators. Now if I want to sample something I either look for material that's explicitly cleared for that use or I try to recreate the vibe myself rather than lifting the actual audio, partly to avoid the legal risk and partly because it pushes me to be more original anyway.

commonMistakes: Assuming sampling is fine as long as it's not commercially released
Not distinguishing between the recording copyright and the composition copyright
Treating the question as purely legal with no personal or creative reflection
followUps: Do you think the rules around sampling are fair to newer artists working with a limited budget?

question: What do you understand about immersive or spatial audio formats like Dolby Atmos, and why do you think the industry is moving toward them?
lookingFor: Awareness of a current, important industry direction and a reasoned sense of why it matters beyond just being a buzzword.

bullets: Explain the basic idea of object-based, three-dimensional audio versus fixed stereo or surround channels
Give a reason the industry is investing in it, such as streaming platform support or headphone-based binaural playback
Show some personal curiosity or exposure, even if limited
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: As I understand it, Dolby Atmos moves away from mixing to a fixed number of channels, like stereo or 5.1, and instead treats sounds as individual objects placed in a three-dimensional space, which then gets rendered differently depending on the playback system, whether that's a cinema, a soundbar, or headphones using binaural rendering. I think streaming platforms pushing Atmos mixes on regular headphones is the real driver, because it means immersive audio isn't just for people with expensive surround setups anymore, it's available to anyone with AirPods. I've only listened to a handful of Atmos mixes myself so far, but the sense of sounds moving around rather than just left to right genuinely surprised me the first time I heard it done well.

commonMistakes: Confusing Atmos with simple stereo widening or reverb effects
Naming the format with no explanation of why it's spreading now
Overstating hands-on experience they don't actually have
followUps: What challenges do you think mixing in an object-based format creates compared to a traditional stereo mix?

subtopic: Sound design for film or games
question: Have you done any sound design work for visual media, like film, a game, or an animation? What was the challenge in matching sound to picture?
lookingFor: Evidence of experimenting outside pure music production, and understanding that sound design serves narrative and timing constraints music alone doesn't have.

bullets: Describe a specific project, even a small or amateur one, and what it required
Identify a real challenge tied to timing, mood, or storytelling rather than pure sound quality
Reflect on how it differs from writing music for its own sake
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I scored a short film a friend made for a school project, about four minutes long, and the hardest part wasn't writing the music itself but getting the timing to feel invisible, a cue coming in half a second late completely broke the emotional beat even though musically it was the same material. I also had to build some foley-style sounds for a scene with no dialogue, footsteps and a door creak, using household objects recorded close to a mic, which taught me how much texture matters more than realism for selling an effect. It made me realise sound design is really about serving someone else's story rather than expressing my own taste, which is a different discipline from writing a track I just want to sound good on its own.

commonMistakes: Describing only music composition with no actual sound design or foley element
No mention of timing or narrative constraints specific to visual media
Claiming professional-level experience that wouldn't hold up under follow-up
followUps: How did you decide what to leave out of the soundtrack, not just what to include?

question: Pick a track whose production you find really impressive. What specifically makes it well made, technically?
lookingFor: Genuinely critical, technically literate listening rather than just naming a favourite song.

bullets: Name a specific track and identify one or two concrete production choices, not just 'it sounds good'
Use correct technical vocabulary appropriately, such as space, arrangement, or dynamics
Show they've listened analytically, perhaps on headphones or picking apart a section
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I keep coming back to Billie Eilish's 'bury a friend', particularly how much empty space is in the mix, the low sub-bass hits sit almost completely alone with barely any competing frequencies, so when they land they feel enormous even though the track isn't loud in the conventional sense. There's also that vocal chop used almost as a percussive element rather than a melodic one, panned hard and processed to sound almost mechanical, which creates tension against how intimate and close her lead vocal is. Listening on headphones, I noticed how much of the low end is mono while the higher, weirder textures are spread wide, which I think is a big part of why the track feels both huge and unsettling at the same time.

commonMistakes: Naming a favourite song with only emotional, non-technical reasons
Using technical jargon incorrectly or without real understanding
Describing the song's lyrics or meaning instead of its production
followUps: Is there a specific technique from that track you'd want to try in your own work?

question: Music technology sits between musical and technical skill. Where would you say your strengths currently lie, and what are you weaker at?
lookingFor: Honest self-assessment across both dimensions of the field, showing awareness of what the course will actually demand.

bullets: Give an honest, specific account of relative strength on the musical side
Give an honest, specific account of relative strength or weakness on the technical side
Show a plan or willingness to close the gap rather than dismissing the weaker area
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: I'd say my musicianship is stronger right now, I've played piano for eight years and I can hear when an arrangement isn't working even if I can't always articulate why technically. My technical side is newer, I'm confident in a DAW but I've never touched real signal flow with outboard gear or patchbays, and my theory around acoustics is mostly self-taught and patchy. I know that gap needs closing, which is honestly a big part of why I want a structured course rather than continuing to teach myself piecemeal from videos.

commonMistakes: Claiming to be equally strong at everything with no real self-critique
Dismissing one side of the field as unimportant to justify a weakness
Giving a vague answer with no specific skills named on either side
followUps: What have you actually done to try to close that gap yourself so far?

question: Why does room acoustics matter when recording or mixing, and what's the difference between soundproofing and acoustic treatment?
lookingFor: Understanding that acoustic treatment shapes sound inside a room while soundproofing stops sound leaving or entering it, and that confusing the two is a common beginner mistake.

bullets: Explain that untreated rooms create reflections that colour a recording or mislead a mix decision
Distinguish acoustic treatment, shaping sound within the room, from soundproofing, blocking sound transfer
Give a concrete example of a problem caused by poor room acoustics
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Room acoustics matter because any untreated space adds its own reflections and resonances on top of whatever you're recording or mixing on, so what you're hearing isn't purely the instrument or the speakers, it's that plus the room. A common beginner mistake, which I made myself, is buying foam panels thinking they'll stop noise getting into the neighbours' flat, when actually that's soundproofing, a completely different job usually involving mass and sealing gaps, while acoustic treatment like foam or bass traps just controls reflections inside the room. I found this out when I mixed a track in an untreated bedroom that had a bass buildup in one corner, and the mix translated terribly on other speakers because I'd been compensating for a problem that wasn't actually in the music.

commonMistakes: Confusing soundproofing and acoustic treatment as the same thing
No concrete example of how poor acoustics caused a real problem
Vague statement that 'the room matters' with no explanation of why
followUps: What's a bass trap, and why is low end usually the hardest problem in a small room?

question: Music technology graduates go into everything from studio engineering to game audio to instrument design. What direction interests you, and how does this course help you get there?
lookingFor: A grounded, specific direction that shows research into the field's actual career paths, with a clear line back to what the course offers.

bullets: Name a specific direction within the broad field, not just 'something in music'
Show awareness that this is one of several real paths the field offers
Connect it honestly to a specific part of the course, while showing flexibility
idealAnswer.modelAnswer: Right now I'm most drawn to game audio, implementing adaptive music and sound design that reacts to what a player is actually doing, rather than a fixed linear score, which is a completely different puzzle from writing a normal song. I know that's a competitive and quite technical corner of the field, closer to programming than a lot of people expect, which is exactly why your course's interactive audio module and the middleware training stood out to me when I researched it. I'm realistic that my interests might shift once I'm exposed to studio work or live sound properly, and I'd rather keep that door open than lock myself into one path before I've tried the others.

commonMistakes: Giving an overly vague answer like 'I want to work in the music industry'
Naming a career path with no connection to any specific part of the course
Sounding so fixed on one path that they seem inflexible or under-informed about alternatives
followUps: What's put you off any of the other paths in this field, if anything?
